Results

1 METHODS

1.1 Outcome Measures

The primary outcome assessed was change in depression or anxiety symptom severity measured with a validated rating scale (e.g., Beck Depression Inventory, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Secondary outcomes included pre–post changes in serum micronutrient concentrations and adverse events. Studies that did not report sufficient quantitative outcome data were excluded.

Given that different scales were used across trials, outcomes were standardized using standardized mean differences (SMDs). When multiple scales were reported for the same condition within a study, the most commonly used scale across studies was selected. A complete list of scales and their frequency of use is provided in the appendix.

1.2 Statistical Analysis

Analysis was conducted using a Bayesian network meta-analysis that combined direct and indirect comparisons under a hierarchical random-effects model with study-level random effects. Models were fit using the brms package in R, which implements Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling via Stan to estimate posterior distributions of treatment effects. Additional model details are provided in the Appendix (Appendix ##).

The assumption of transitivity may be threatened by uneven distributions of baseline vitamin deficiency and baseline depression or anxiety status across interventions. We therefore evaluated transitivity by examining whether key potential effect modifiers were similarly distributed across treatment comparisons. Specifically, we assessed sex distribution, baseline micronutrient deficiency, and baseline symptom severity, each of which may plausibly influence treatment response. Study- and comparison-level characteristics were visually inspected to identify systematic imbalances across the network. In addition, prespecified network meta-regression models were used to formally evaluate effect modification by these study-level characteristics, and subgroup-specific estimates are reported.

A common between-study heterogeneity parameter (τ) was assumed across interventions within each outcome network. Heterogeneity was interpreted by comparing τ to the scale of observed treatment effects and by examining prediction intervals. Coherence (consistency) was assessed using node-splitting models and a design-by-treatment interaction model. Residual heterogeneity and inconsistency were further explored using prespecified meta-regression models evaluating potential sources of variability, including risk of bias, baseline symptom severity, baseline micronutrient levels, year and country of study, standard error, and duration of follow-up (Appendix ##). Contour-enhanced funnel plots were used to assess potential small-study effects.

Certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework, which assesses six domains: within-study bias, across-studies bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, and incoherence (Nikolakopoulou, 2020). Confidence ratings were generated for all interventions relative to placebo and for all contrasts present in the network (Appendix ##).

2 RESULTS

2.1 Study Selection

Using our selection criteria, we identified 5036 records. After excluding 1886 duplicates, 3150 records underwent title and abstract screening. Of these, 2849 were excluded for not meeting eligibility criteria. We assessed 301 full-text articles and excluded 190 due to an ineligible intervention, unavailable full text, use of a non-validated measure of depression or anxiety, duplicate data, or inadequate reporting for analysis. We included 111 studies for data extraction, excluding 10 for failing to meet inclusion criteria or lacking usable data. A total of 101 studies were included in our analyses—both main and sensitivity—with 50 studies in the main analysis and 51 included in sensitivity analyses only. The study selection process is outlined in the PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1).

2.2 Characteristics of Included Studies

The 101 included studies were published between 1973 and 2024. Interventions comprised B vitamins (26 studies), vitamin C (3), vitamin D (45), zinc (12), magnesium (11), selenium (3), iron (2), and multi-nutrient combinations (30), each evaluated alone or in combination. Eighteen studies considered antidepressant treatment in addition to treatment with micronutrients. Follow-up ranged from 4 weeks to 7.2 years (median 12 weeks). Most studies assessed depressive symptoms (n = 94, 93.1%), whereas fewer evaluated anxiety (n = 32, 31.7%).

Among the 50 low risk-of-bias studies, 12 examined B vitamins, 1 vitamin C, 32 vitamin D, 3 zinc, 3 magnesium, 2 selenium, and 2 iron (each alone or in combination), with 13 evaluating multi-nutrient combinations. Follow-up ranged from 6 weeks to 5 years (median 12 weeks). All assessed depressive symptoms (n = 50, 100%), and fewer assessed anxiety (n = 18, 36%). Additional characteristics are shown in Table ## (Appendix ##).

2.3 Population Characteristics

Overall, 37,932 participants were included, with study sample sizes ranging from 6 to 10,662. Of these, 33,640 were from low risk-of-bias studies. A total of 34,118 participants completed follow-up, corresponding to an overall attrition rate of 10.1%.

Among low risk-of-bias studies, 30,050 participants completed follow-up (range 11 to 9,226), with an attrition rate of 10.7%. These studies were more likely to account for missing data (typically last observation carried forward); none used multiple imputation. In low risk-of-bias studies, the mean age was 64.65 years (range 21.45–79.3), with 49.7% male participants.

Across all studies (n = 101), 95 (100%) reported at least one baseline micronutrient level. Among low risk-of-bias studies, 50 (100%) reported baseline levels; 11 (22%) measured one micronutrient and 33 measured two. Among low risk-of-bias studies, weighted mean baseline concentrations were: vitamin B9 8.10 ng/mL, red blood cell B9 300.17 ng/mL, vitamin B12 365.82 pg/mL, vitamin D 22.56 ng/mL, zinc 83.55 ug/dL, magnesium 3.10 mg/dL, selenium 61.00 ug/L, and ferritin 65.54 ng/mL.

Vitamins B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, and C were not measured in low risk-of-bias studies, either because baseline levels were not assessed or because measurements occurred only in studies excluded from the main analysis due to higher risk of bias.

Sex distribution and baseline clinical status varied across comparisons, with some interventions evaluated primarily in female or clinically depressed populations. The distribution of key study-level characteristics across the network is summarized in the Appendix (Appendix ##).

2.4 Intervention Characteristics

Vitamin D (32 studies) was the most common intervention aside from placebo (the total daily dose ranged from 600 IU to 14286 IU; and the duration of supplementation ranged from 6 weeks to 5 years).

B vitamins (12 studies) included B1 (the total daily dose was 300 mg; and the duration of supplementation was 12 weeks), B6 (the total daily dose ranged from 25 mg to 40 mg; and the duration of supplementation ranged from 8 weeks to 5 years), B9 (the total daily dose ranged from 0 mg to 5 mg; and the duration of supplementation ranged from 8 weeks to 5 years), and B12 (the total daily dose ranged from 100 ug to 500 ug; and the duration of supplementation ranged from 1 year to 5 years).

Vitamin C (1 study) was evaluated at the total daily dose was 500 mg for and the duration of supplementation was 8 weeks.

Minerals included zinc (3; the total daily dose ranged from 37 mg to 150 mg; and the duration of supplementation ranged from 8 to 12 weeks), magnesium (3; the total daily dose ranged from 150 mg to 500 mg; and the duration of supplementation ranged from 8 to 12 weeks), selenium (2; the total daily dose was 200 ug; and the duration of supplementation was 12 weeks), and iron (2; the total daily dose ranged from 9 mg to 27 mg; and the duration of supplementation ranged from 12 weeks to 1 year).

13 studies evaluated multi-nutrient combinations, most commonly B12, B9, and D.

2.5 Risk of Bias Within Studies

52 studies were rated low risk (51.49%), 18 had unclear risk (17.82%), and 31 were high risk (30.69%). The most frequent sources of bias were selective outcome reporting. Primary analyses were restricted to low risk-of-bias studies. Domain-level assessments are shown in Figure 2.

2.6 Effect of Micronutrient Supplementation on Depression Symptoms

In analyses restricted to studies at low overall risk of bias, only vitamin D and selenium yielded posterior mean estimates with 95% credible intervals excluding the null (Figure 4).

For vitamin D, the posterior mean effect was -0.32 standard deviations compared with placebo (95% CrI, -0.51 to -0.13). For context, assuming a standard deviation of approximately 9 points on the Beck Depression Inventory, this corresponds to roughly a 3-point greater improvement relative to placebo; because multiple depression scales were used across studies, this translation is intended as an illustrative approximation.

The posterior mean effect for selenium was larger in magnitude (-0.99 standard deviations; 95% CrI, -1.9 to -0.11), but was informed by only 2 studies (N = 122), and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

Other micro-nutrients, including vitamin B6 (SMD -0.92, 95% CrI: -2.27 to 0.41) and vitamin B1 (SMD -0.6, 95% CrI: -1.68 to 0.51), showed point estimates suggestive of benefit; however, credible intervals were wide and included the null (Figure 4). CINeMA ratings indicated low confidence for selenium and very low confidence for all other comparisons (See the appendix).

Between-study heterogeneity was substantial: the posterior mean of \tau was 0.45 (95% CrI: 0.29 to 0.63), comparable in magnitude to some estimated treatment effects.

Given the uneven distribution of baseline deficiency and depression status across interventions, subgroup and meta-regression analyses were conducted to evaluate potential effect modification. In meta-regression models, baseline deficiency and baseline depression were associated with larger estimated effects of vitamin D. Among populations that were both depressed and vitamin D deficient, the posterior mean effect was -0.49 (95% CrI: -0.74 to -0.25). In depressed but non-deficient populations, the estimate was similar in magnitude but more uncertain (-0.49, 95% CrI: -1.11 to 0.09). In depressed populations with unknown deficiency status, the posterior mean effect was -1.02 (95% CrI: -1.89 to -0.14). In non-depressed populations, estimated effects were close to null regardless of deficiency status. CINeMA ratings for vitamin D estimates for depressed populations were rated as low confidence while those in non-depressed populations were rated as very low confidence (see the appendix).

For selenium, subgroup estimates were based on minimal data. In a deficient, non-depressed population (one study), the posterior mean effect was -2.96 (95% CrI: -4.22 to -1.7). This estimate was rated as moderate confidence following the CINeMA guidelines. In a depressed population with unknown deficiency status (one study), the estimate was 0.01 (95% CrI: -0.89 to 0.9). This estimate was rated as very low confidence following CINeMA guidelines. Results for other vitamins are provided in the Appendix.

Dose–response analyses suggested a possible gradient for vitamin D, although credible intervals overlapped across dose categories. For doses <1000 IU/day, the mean difference was (95% CrI: to ), compared with and at higher dose categories (full estimates in Appendix). Longer study duration was generally associated with attenuation toward the null, though estimates were imprecise. Vitamin D effects were largest in studies ≤8 weeks and diminished in longer-duration categories (see Sensitivity Analyses for full estimates).

In low risk-of-bias analyses, antidepressant augmentation trials formed a disconnected sub-network and were therefore modeled separately, with antidepressant monotherapy as the reference. These estimates did not contribute to indirect comparisons in the primary network. Augmentation effects were similar in magnitude to antidepressant monotherapy but were based on few studies. For example, only 3 studies evaluated vitamin D augmentation (SMD: -0.28, 95% CrI: -1.08 to 0.49), while 2 studies examined antidepressants plus vitamin B9 (SMD: -0.55, 95% CrI: -1.23 to 0.19). Similarly, 1 study examined antidepressants plus vitamin B6, B9, and B12 (SMD: -0.45, 95% CrI: -1.44 to 0.56).

2.7 Effect of Micronutrient Supplementation on Anxiety Symptoms

Among studies at low overall risk of bias, no examined vitamins or minerals had 95% credible intervals excluding the null. The largest estimated effect was observed for selenium (SMD -0.24, 95% CrI: -0.79 to 0.48); in contrast to its effect on depression, vitamin D was estimated to have little average effect on anxiety symptoms. Only one low risk-of-bias study evaluated antidepressant augmentation with vitamin D for anxiety, so this estimate is not presented. All estimates were rated as very low confidence according to CINeMA guidelines (see the appendix).

The posterior mean of \tau in the anxiety network was 0.34 (95% CrI: 0.05 to 0.68). Despite largely null effects, heterogeneity was substantial.

Subgroup estimates by baseline deficiency and baseline anxiety status also yielded no comparisons with credible intervals excluding the null. For vitamin D, the posterior mean effect in deficient populations with baseline anxiety was -0.02 (95% CrI: -0.47 to 0.41), and in non-deficient populations with baseline anxiety was 0.03 (95% CrI: -0.96 to 0.94). No studies assessed vitamin D for anxiety in populations with unknown deficiency status. Results for other vitamins are provided in the Appendix. All estimates were rated as very low confidence following CINeMA guidelines.

No clear patterns were observed in duration- or dose-stratified analyses (Appendix).

4 Protocol

The protocol for this review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024575661) and is available at [https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024575661]. The protocol was developed in accordance with PRISMA-P guidelines and included detailed plans for literature search, study selection, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and statistical analysis. Any deviations from the protocol are described in the Methods section of this report.

4.1 Post-hoc analyses

Given the restrictiveness of setting a whole population as deficient vs non-deficient, we will also consider meta-regression analyses using continuous measures of baseline deficiency where available such a estimated percent deficient. This will rely on the assumption of a log-Normal distribution to calculate these probabilities.

Similarly for baseline depression and anxiety status, we will estimate percent of the population that is depressed or anxious at baseline using a log-Normal distribution.

6.2 Rating scales

The depression scales used across studies included BDI-I, GDS-15, MADRS, EPDS, DASS-21, depression, BDI-II, HADS-D, CES-D, PHQ-9, HRS, and HAM-D. The anxiety scales used included DASS-21, anxiety, HADS-A, STAI-S, BAI, HAM-A, and PANAS. The frequency of each table are presented in the tables below.

6.3 Coding decisions for data extraction

Most studies measured baseline depression status on the above validated scales and several studies measured baseline micro-nutrient status of the vitamin being repleted. However, to ease comparison between studies, we dichotomized these measures. For baseline depression status, we categorized studies as including a depressed population if the average baseline score on the primary depression scale used in the study met or exceeded the standard cutoff for mild depression. For baseline micro-nutrient status, we categorized studies as including a deficient population if they measured baseline levels of the vitamin being repleted and the average level was in the deficient range according to standard clinical cutoffs. These categorizations were used in subgroup and meta-regression analyses to evaluate potential effect modification by baseline depression and micro-nutrient status. These particular cutoffs are detailed in the tables below.

Further, cross-over trials were permissible in our study but we only used the first period of randomization before cross-over to avoid carry-over effects. In studies with multiple active arms, we combined active arms together when appropriate to avoid double counting the placebo arm. In studies with multiple control arms, we selected the most appropriate control arm for comparison with the active arm(s) based on the study design and characteristics of the control arms.

7 Statistical Methods in Detail

7.1 Measures of Treatment Effects

The effect size for our studies was the standardized mean difference (SMD). This was selected because the included studies in our analysis use a variety of different depression and anxiety scales (See @app-rating-scales). We preferred utilizing regression estimates when available and relevant followed by gain scores and finally end point measures. To transform these into SMDs, we calculated the SMD following Hedge’s g (Hedge year). When studies provided medians, interquartile ranges, and minima and maxima we calculated an estimate of the mean using the methods described in Wan et al. (2014). In most networks considered in the analysis, placebo was the reference treatment. In the antidepressant network, we used treatment with any kind of antidepressant (TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs, etc.) as the reference treatment.

Missing standard deviations were handled in a few ways when possible. First, some studies reported standard errors so these were transformed into standard deviations using the usual formula. Second, if both were missing but confidence intervals, t-values, or p-values were available we used the methods described in Section 7.7.3 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews (Higgins 2008). Finally, if only medians were available and the study reported either the interquartile range or range, we estimated the standard deviation following the method described in Wan et al. (2014).

7.2 Network Meta-Analysis Model Specification

We fitted our Bayesian network meta-analysis and meta-regression models using the brms package in R to interface with the Stan sampling language. We accounted for correlations between multi-arm studies by assuming a correlation parameter of 0.5 between arms of the same study.

using the brms functionality for multivariate meta-analysis. We used weakly informative priors for all parameters and conducted sensitivity analyses to evaluate the impact of different prior choices on our results. The details of the model specification, including the likelihood, random effects structure, and priors, are described in the sections below.

7.2.1 Likelihood

The likelihood for our network meta-analysis model was specified as follows for each outcome (depression and anxiety:

For all studies i = 1, \dots, N and treatment arms j = 1, \dots, J_{i}, we observed effect sizes y_{i,j} or the i-th study and j-th treatment arm with corresponding variances \sigma_{i,j}^2:

y_{i,1}, y_{i,2}, \ldots, y_{i,J_{i}} \sim \text{Multivariate Student-t}\left(\mathbf{\mu}_i, \Sigma_i, \nu \right),

where \mathbf{\mu} is the vector of true effect sizes for each treatment arm, \Sigma_i is the covariance matrix for study i that accounts for the within-study correlations between arms, and \nu = 30 is the degrees of freedom parameter for the Student-t distribution which allows for heavier tails to account for potential outliers. The covariance matrix \Sigma_i was specified as \sigma_{i,j}^2 on the diagonal and \sigma_{i,0}^2 for the off-diagonal elements where \sigma_{i,0} is the standard deviation of the reference arm for the trial. Note that J_i is one less than the total number of arms in the trial, as the reference arm is not included in the likelihood.

The vector \mathbf{\mu}_i of true effect sizes for study i corresponds to the treatment effects for each arm relative to a reference treatment (e.g., placebo) and was modeled as a function of the treatment effects, \theta and random effects, \upsilon as described in the next section. for example, for a study where the first arm compared treatment A to B, it’s mean component would be equal to \theta_A - \theta_B + \upsilon_{i,1}.

For the same arm in the same study, the mean for the effect modifier analysis including deficiency status and baseline depression/anxiety status would be calculated as

\begin{aligned} \theta_A - \theta_B &+ \alpha_A \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{disease}_i = \text{yes}) - \alpha_B \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{disease}_i = \text{yes}) \\ &+ \delta_A \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{deficient}_i = \text{yes}) - \delta_B \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{deficient} = \text{yes}) \\ &+ \gamma_A \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{disease}_i = \text{yes}) \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{disease}_i = \text{yes}) \\ &- \gamma_B \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{deficient}_i = \text{yes}) \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{disease}_i = \text{yes}) + \upsilon_i \end{aligned}

In our meta regression analysis, the same mean function would hold except we would also include confounders, X, in a standard linear regression term: X\beta.

7.2.2 Random Effects Structure

We specified a random effects structure to account for between-study heterogeneity in treatment effects. For each study i with J_i arms,

\upsilon_i \sim N(0, \tau^2 R_i), where R is a J_i \times J_i correlation matrix with 1’s on the diagonal and \rho for the off-diagonal elements, where \rho is the assumed correlation between treatment effects within the same study. We set \rho = 0.5 based on previous literature and expert consensus on typical correlations in multi-arm trials. The parameter \tau represents the between-study variance in treatment effects and was estimated from the data.

7.2.3 Priors

We set a prior on effect sizes of \theta \sim N(0, 2.5^2) with the same prior on effect modifiers \delta and \alpha. We took \tau \sim N_+(0, 0.5^2), a half-normal prior which is commonly used for variance parameters in random effects.

In our meta regression, we put a regularized prior as described in the BRMS documentation on \beta to help prevent overfitting given the large number of covariates and relatively small number of studies (Carvalho, 2009; Piironen 2017):

\beta_1, \ldots \beta_K \sim \text{regularized-horseshoe}(\text{df} = 3, \text{global scale} = 0.1, \text{scale slab} = 1).

Other parameters in the meta-regression were estimated as random effects, such as the effect of country of study and the effect of scale used, and these were given the same half-normal prior as \tau.

7.2.4 Other details of meta-regression

Several studies did not measure either sex or age, so we imputed the mean age and percent male in these studies. We utilized regression models in brms to jointly model our meta-regression as well as predict these missing covariates. To ease in sampling for Stan, we normalized continuous variables to have mean 0 and standard deviation of 1.

One important facet of the meta-regression is that we included an Egger regression term to account for potential small study effects and publication bias. This term is a function of the standard error of the effect size and allows us to evaluate whether there is evidence of small study effects in our data. We allowed this term to vary by country of study to account for potential differences in publication bias across different regions.

7.2.5 Assessment of convergence

To monitor convergence, we examined trace plots for all parameters and calculated the potential scale reduction factor (Rhat) for each parameter. We considered Rhat values below 1.05 as indicative of good convergence. We also examined the effective sample size for each parameter to ensure that we had sufficient sampling to obtain stable estimates.

7.2.6 Software

We utilize R version 4.5.1 for analyses. The brms package version 2.23.0 was used to fit the Bayesian network meta-analysis and meta-regression models, which interfaces with the Stan sampling language. We utilized the cmdstanr version 0.9.0.9000 backend to sample from the posterior distributions. The tidyverse suite of packages was used for data manipulation and visualization, and the gt package was used for creating tables.

8 Assessment of Quality

8.1 Network geometry

The network between the full data differs from the low bias data in that all treatments are fully connected in a simple analysis, whereas in the low bias data antidepressant treatments are disconnected from the rest of the network. This is largely because there were no low bias studies comparing antidepressant treatment to placebo or to another micronutrient. The network geometry for the low bias data is presented in Figure 3.

Given the suspected effect modification by baseline deficiency and depression/anxiety status, we also examined the network geometry broken out by these characteristics. The network geometry for low bias studies broken out by deficiency and depression/anxiety status is presented in Figure 7 and Figure 8. We can see that some caution needs to be taken in interpreting simple analyses as some comparisons are informed by studies with different distributions of baseline deficiency and depression/anxiety status. For example, the comparison of vitamin B9 to placebo is informed by a couple of studies in depressed and non-deficient populations across all data, but no studies in non-depressed or deficient populations.

8.4 Assessment of Transitivity

The assumption of transitivity was evaluated by examining whether potential effect modifiers were similarly distributed across treatment comparisons. Based on clinical and methodological considerations, we identified baseline micro-nutrient deficiency status, baseline depression/anxiety severity, age, and sex as effect modifiers.

We summarized the distribution of these characteristics across treatment comparisons and visually inspected network diagrams stratified by deficiency and depression status. In addition, meta-regression models incorporating deficiency status and depression status were fitted to assess whether treatment effects varied systematically according to these characteristics. Node splitting further assessed inconsistency between direct and indirect evidence for comparisons with both direct and indirect evidence.

When examining the effect of placebo over time, there did not appear to be any major trend in response to placebo over time either by gain score or final endpoint mean. We ran random effects models adjusting for scale used and attempted to use varying slopes by scale but the variance of the slope random effect was estimated to be zero. Overall, we found very small changes in placebo response over time that were not statistically significant. On average, the end points trended downward while the gain scores trended upward. The mean placebo response over time is presented in Figure 18 and Figure 19.

8.5 Reporting bias

8.5.1 Funnel plots for main analysis

We assessed reporting bias by examining funnel plots both for the simple model without effect modification and for the model including effect modification by baseline deficiency and depression/anxiety status. The funnel plots for the simple model are presented in Figure 20 and Figure 21. The funnel plots for the model including effect modification are presented in Figure 22 and Figure 23.

Based on the funnel plots, there is some evidence of asymmetry in the simple model for depression and a anxiety outcomes, which may suggest the presence of small study effects or publication bias. The models incorporating baseline disease (depression/anxiety) and deficiency status appear more symmetric but still appear to have outliers. Thus, we also examined funnel plots by intervention to further explore potential sources of asymmetry. The funnel plots for the simple model by intervention are presented in Figure 24 and Figure 25. The funnel plots for the model including effect modification by intervention are presented in Figure 26 and Figure 27.

8.5.2 Funnel plots for all data

We also examined funnel plots for all data to assess reporting bias in the full dataset. The funnel plots for the simple model in all data are presented in Figure 28 and Figure 29. The funnel plots for the model including effect modification in all data are presented in Figure 30 and Figure 31.

8.5.3 Publication bias assessment by country

In this section we present the evidence from our meta-regression analyses as to whether there are any country level effects (1) in general and (2) with publication bias. We utilize a Egger regression (regression of the standard error of estimates on the outcome) with a random effect by country to assess whether there is evidence of small study effects by country. We also present funnel plots highlighting studies from Iran, which had the largest number of studies and thus may be driving any observed small study effects. The results of the meta-regression analyses are presented in Figure 32 and the funnel plots are presented in Figure 33 and Figure 34.

Contour enhanced funnel plot with studies centered by meta-regression adjusted estimates (\hat{\mu}) for depression and anxiety outcomes. Compared to the funnel plots above, there appear to be fewer outliers. SMD = Standardized mean difference.

Contour enhanced funnel plot by intervention with studies centered by meta-regression adjusted estimates (\hat{\mu}) for depression and anxiety outcomes. Compared to the funnel plots above, there appear to be fewer outliers. SMD = Standardized mean difference.

8.6 Inconsistency assessment

The assessment of inconsistency involved comparing direct and indirect evidence for each comparison in the network. This was done in two ways.

First, a design-by-treatment interaction model was fitted to the data, which tests for inconsistency across the entire network. If there was a significant design-by-treatment interaction, this was considered evidence of inconsistency in the network.

This was done using node-splitting models, which separate the evidence for a particular comparison into direct and indirect components and test for differences between them. If there was a significant difference between the direct and indirect estimates for a comparison, this was considered evidence of inconsistency. The results of the node-splitting analyses are presented in Figure 35 and Figure 36.

8.7 Heterogeneity assessments

Heterogeneity was assessed by examining the posterior distribution of the heterogeneity parameter (\tau) from the network meta-analysis models. The mean and 95% credible interval for \tau are reported in the results section. A larger value of \tau indicates greater heterogeneity between studies.

To get a sense of the scale of heterogeneity, we also report the 95% prediction interval for the treatment effects, which incorporates both the uncertainty in the estimated treatment effects and the heterogeneity between studies. If the prediction interval is wide and includes both clinically meaningful benefits and harms, this suggests that there is substantial heterogeneity in the treatment effects across studies. We set a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 0.5 standardized mean difference for both depression and anxiety outcomes, based on previous literature on the interpretation of standardized mean differences in mental health research (e.g., Cuijpers et al., 2014; Furukawa et al., 2014). If the prediction interval includes values greater than 0.5 or less than -0.5, this suggests that there is substantial heterogeneity in the treatment effects across studies.

Prediction intervals for the main model in the paper assessing the effects of micro-nutrients on anxiety The plot shows the estimated treatment effects (standardized mean differences) for each comparison in the network meta-analysis, along with 95% credible intervals (in black) and 95% prediction intervals (in red). The prediction intervals are wider than the credible intervals, reflecting the additional uncertainty due to heterogeneity between studies. If the prediction interval includes values greater than 0.5 or less than -0.5, this suggests that there is substantial heterogeneity in the treatment effects across studies.

10 Meta-regression Results

In this section we present the evidence from our meta-regression analyses assessing potential effect modification by baseline depression/anxiety status and baseline micro-nutrient deficiency status.

10.1 Fixed effects for depression outcomes

10.1.1 Cumulative ranking plots

10.2 Fixed effects for anxiety outcomes

11 Sensitivity Analyses

11.6 Percent Deficient and Percent with Baseline Disease Status

In our main analysis, we classify studies as being in deficient (or non-deficient) populations based strictly on the mean value of the baseline micro-nutrient level. However, since this is a population level distinction and there would be many people without deficiency (respectively, with deficiency) in the deficient (respectively, non-deficient) populations. Thus, we wanted to assess treatment effects if we tried to better account for the real population percentages.

To do so, we assume a log-Gaussian distribution to calculate the percentages of deficient and non-deficient participants in each study based on the reported mean and standard deviation of baseline micro-nutrient levels. We do the same for the percentage of participants with baseline depression or anxiety symptoms based on the reported mean and standard deviation of baseline symptom severity.

Some studies didn’t report enough information to calculate these percentages, so their values were imputed using a simple truncated Gaussian model with only an intercept and a term for year of publication.

We should note that the probabilities from the log-Gaussian distribution, if underestimated, would expect the results to be biased away from the null; if overestimated, the results would be biased toward the null. Thus, the results of this analysis should be interpreted with caution as they are based on assumptions about the distribution of micro-nutrient levels and symptom severity in the included studies.

11.6.1 Results for Depression Outcomes

For vitamin D, there is some evidence that higher percentages of participants with baseline vitamin D deficiency were associated with larger treatment effects. There also appears to be an interaction with depression status. The results for vitamin D are presented graphically in Figure 65. Most interventions only had one study for estimation so that most terms in the model would not be identifiable. 11.1 Gaussian likelihood vs Student-t likelihood

We assessed the fit of a typical Gaussian likelihood versus a robust Student-t likelihood using leave-one-out cross validation. The results are presented in Table 17 and Table 18. In all cases, the Student-t likelihood had a better fit than the Gaussian likelihood, perhaps suggesting that there were some outliers in the data.

11.2 All measures vs only endline measures

We assessed the fit of models using best available outcome measure (regression estimates, gain scores, endpoint scores) versus only endpoint measures using leave-one-out cross validation. The results between the two models were very similar.

11.3 Leave-One-Out Estimates

In addition to comparing leave-one-out (LOO) comparing model fit, we also calculated the change in treatment effect estimates when leaving out each study in turn. The results are presented in Figure 51 and Figure 52. If the leave-one-out estimates are similar to the overall estimate and do not show large deviations, this suggests that no single study has a disproportionate influence on the overall results.

11.3.2 Leave-one-out estimates with all data

11.4 Dose Response Estimates

Part of our interest was to assess whether any dose response relationship existed between micro-nutrient supplementation and depression and anxiety outcomes. To do this, we followed the method of Watt et al. and estimated dose categories as a random effect (Watt 2022). This eliminates the need for complex modeling of the dose response curve and will also pool estimates toward the grand mean if data do not support them being different. The dose categories chose for each micro-nutrient were based on the distribution of doses in the included studies and clinical relevance. For example, for vitamin D, we categorized doses as low (<1000 IU/day), medium (1000-3000 IU/day), and high (>3000 IU/day). We then estimated the treatment effect for each dose category compared to placebo. This method also allowed us to include several additional studies that did not have a true comparison group but simply compared different doses of micro-nutrients, such as Penckofer et al. (2022) that used total daily doses of vitamin D about 700 IU versus 7000 IU. Full dose categories for micro-nutrients are presented in @tab-dose-cat.

11.5 Duration Estimates

To assess whether the duration of treatment was associated with treatment effects, we estimated the treatment by duration categories as a random effect. The duration categories were initially selected at 0-4 weeks, 4-8 weeks, and >8 weeks; however, given the actual distribution of study durations, we combined the 0-4 weeks and 4-8 weeks categories and separated the >8 week into 8-16 weeks, 16-26 weeks and > 26 weeks. The results are presented in @tab-duration-response-dep and @tab-duration-response-anx. Only vitamin D had studies in each duration category so we present it’s results graphically. In low bias data, there is significant uncertainty but there does seem to be evidence of attenuation in treatment effects over time. Vitamin D figures presented in Figure 61 and Figure 62.

12 Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis Ratings

Our judgments below are based on the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework of Nikolakopoulou et al. (2018).

12.1 Reasons for downgrading

1. Within-study bias

We assessed within-study bias using the Risk of Bias 1 (ROB) tool (Higgins et al., 2011). Studies were evaluated among the seven domains of bias: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, and other sources of bias. Each domain was rated as low risk, unclear risk, or high risk of bias. Only studies with an overall rating of “low risk” were included in our primary analyses. Bias was assessed by two authors with a third member breaking any ties.

The rating for the overall risk of bias for a comparison was measured as the average bias of all studies contributing to the comparison as weighted by the contribution matrix.

Bias assessments for all studies are presented in Figure 9 and Figure 10. The most common sources of bias were selective outcome reporting.

2. Reporting bias

Our search included over 3000 studies from Ovid MEDLINE, Embase.com, Web of Science Core Collection, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and APA PsycINFO databases. Given this, we think it is unlikely that there are many large studies that were missed in our search. However, we cannot rule out the possibility of some smaller studies being missed, particularly those published in non-English languages or those published in less accessible journals. Thus, any other evidence of missing studies would likely be do to publication bias.

To assess for publication bias, we examined funnel plots for our primary outcome of depression scales and anxiety scales. Then, if there was evidence of publication bias, we examined funnel plots for each intervention separately. If there were more than 10 studies in a comparison, we would examine the funnel plot for that comparison. If there was evidence of publication bias at the intervention level, then reporting bias was downgraded by one level. For comparisons with 10 or fewer studies, reporting bias was downgraded one level if the global assessment found evidence of reporting bias.

We also conducted meta-regression analyses to examine whether the country in which a study was conducted, the year of publication, the duration of treatment, the baseline severity of symptoms, or the age of participants explained some of the heterogeneity between studies.

3. Indirectness

To assess indirectness, we evaluated the assumption of transitivity by examining the distribution of potential effect modifiers across comparisons in the network. Substantial imbalances in these modifiers would raise concerns about transitivity.

Because our objective was to estimate the effect of micro-nutrient supplementation on depression and anxiety symptoms across populations broadly, we had no strong a priori reason to expect violations of transitivity. However, given the small number of studies informing some comparisons, we prespecified baseline symptom severity and baseline micro-nutrient deficiency status as key potential effect modifiers.

We examined the distribution of these variables across treatment comparisons. If meaningful differences were observed, we considered this evidence of potential intransitivity and downgraded the certainty of evidence for indirectness by one level.

4. Imprecision

We examined the credible intervals for each comparison in the network meta-analysis to assess for imprecision. If the credible interval for a comparison included the null value (SMD of 0), then we downgraded for imprecision by one level. If the credible interval was wide and included both clinically meaningful benefits and harms, then we downgraded for imprecision by two levels. We considered an standardized mean difference of 0.5 to be the threshold for clinical significance (Jakobsen, 2020). Thus, if the credible interval for a comparison included both an SMD of -0.5 and an standardized mean difference of 0.5, then we considered this to be a wide credible interval that included both clinically meaningful benefits and harms and downgraded for imprecision by two levels.

5. Heterogeneity

Heterogeneity was assessed similar to imprecision. We calculated prediction intervals for each comparison, calculated by adding a random effect from a new hypothetical study to the mean estimate from the network meta analysis and calculating the 95% credible intervals. If the prediction interval crossed the null value, then we downgraded for heterogeneity by one level. If the prediction interval was wide and included both clinically meaningful benefits and harms, then we downgraded for heterogeneity by two levels. We again considered an standardized mean difference of 0.5 to be the threshold for clinical significance (Jakobsen, 2020).

6. Incoherence

To assess incoherence, we examined the consistency of direct and indirect evidence for each comparison in the network meta-analysis using the Separate Indirect from Direct Evidence (SIDE) approach (Gerta Rücker, Guido Schwarzer, Ulrike Krahn, Jochem König, Orestis Efthimiou. netmeta: Network Meta-Analysis using Frequentist Methods 2018). If there was a significant inconsistency between direct and indirect evidence for a comparison, then we downgraded for incoherence by one level.

We also assessed the fit of unrelated mean effects (design by treatment interaction) as compared to consistency models to examine for incoherence in the network. If the fit of the unrelated mean effects model was substantially better than the consistency model, then we downgraded for incoherence by one level. If the fit of the unrelated mean effects model was substantially better than the consistency model and there were concerns about the transitivity of the network, then we downgraded for incoherence by two levels. We assessed fit by using the expected predictive log density (EPLD) and from a leave one out cross validation. If the EPLD was higher for the unrelated mean effects model than the consistency model, then we downgraded for incoherence by one level.

12.2 Assessment of overall confidence

We downgraded overall confidence in the evidence by one level for any category marked as “some concerns” and by two levels for any category marked as “high risk of bias” or “Major concerns”. We treated indirectness and incoherence as correlated categories representing transitivity and imprecision and heterogeneity as correlated categories for variability. Inside these categories, we reduced the global ranking by one level if any category therein was “Some concerns” and two levels if any category had “Major concerns”.

13 Data/code availability

All code used for data extraction, analysis, and figure generation is available at https://github.com/ericdunipace/vitamin_meta. The data used in the analyses are also available at this repository.
